title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The core failure here is a training-data acquisition problem: Suno admitted its model was trained on essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack indicated the sources included YouTube, Deezer, and Genius, none of which authorized that use. The failure occurred before deployment, at the data-collection stage, and it propagated forward into the deployed product because the model learned to reproduce recognizable characteristics of specific copyrighted recordings closely enough that plaintiffs could prompt it into generating outputs resembling works by identifiable artists.

The second failure is at inference time. A system trained on unlicensed material and then deployed publicly produced outputs that rights holders and courts found too close to existing recordings. No licensing check, no output-screening mechanism, and no rights-clearance process was in place between a user's prompt and the generated audio. Catching this would have required either licensed training data from the outset or a filtering layer capable of detecting substantial similarity to known recordings before output was returned to users.

What is not established: the lawsuits and class actions are allegations, not findings of liability in most jurisdictions, and the settlements reached with some labels, such as Warner Music Group, are not admissions of wrongdoing. The German court ruling in favor of GEMA is a legal finding in that jurisdiction, but it does not determine the outcome of the separate US proceedings, which remain ongoing.

summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records, have filed lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular artificial intelligence music generators. The labels accuse both companies of illegally scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models. The lawsuits claim that these AI services not only used unauthorized music for training but also directly recreate sections of famous songs. The record labels submitted a massive list of thousands of copyrighted works allegedly scraped from artists like The Beatles, Michael Jackson, Mariah Carey, and many others.

To support their case, the record labels claim they recreated famous songs using both AI generators by entering specific prompts describing musical characteristics. They say they were able to generate multiple outputs that closely resembled or directly copied original songs, including pieces by Chuck Berry and Green Day. One example involved generating a near-identical version of Mariah Carey's holiday hit. The lawsuits were filed in New York against Udio and in Massachusetts against Suno, where Suno is headquartered. Both companies previously claimed their training methods constituted fair use.
